summary: Micah 4 opens with a vision of Zion raised up, nations coming to learn Yahweh’s ways, and weapons remade for farming. The chapter then turns to the gathering of the lame and driven away, the return of dominion to Zion, and the pain of exile as far as Babylon. It ends with hostile nations gathered against Zion, but unaware that Yahweh’s counsel will turn their assembly into judgment.
whyItMatters: This chapter interrupts Micah’s accusations against corrupt leadership with one of the book’s clearest pictures of restoration, peace, and gathered survivors. It also keeps that hope attached to exile, distress, and conflict rather than presenting restoration as an uninterrupted idyll.

context.author: The book heading attributes the word to Micah of Moresheth; the finished arrangement of the book is not fully identified.
context.audience: The speeches address Samaria, Jerusalem, Judah’s towns, rulers, prophets, and the people, while also picturing nations as learners or opponents.
context.date: Micah’s attributed prophetic activity belongs to the eighth century BCE, in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah; the date of the finished book is not supplied.
context.setting: Micah’s concerns center on Israel and Judah, especially Jerusalem and the Judean countryside, under the pressure of Assyrian power and with later expectation of Babylonian exile and restoration.
context.literaryForm: Prophetic poetry made of promises, questions, commands, lament imagery, and visions of future restoration.

outline.heading: Nations stream to Yahweh’s mountain
outline.note: The mountain of Yahweh’s temple is pictured as exalted, and many nations invite one another to learn God’s ways from Zion.

outline.heading: Peace under Yahweh’s judgment
outline.note: Yahweh judges among peoples, weapons become farming tools, and the chapter contrasts the nations’ gods with the community’s resolve to walk in Yahweh’s name.

outline.heading: The lame gathered and ruled from Zion
outline.note: Yahweh promises to assemble the lame and driven away, make them a remnant and strong nation, and restore dominion to the daughter of Jerusalem.

outline.heading: Labor pains and Babylon
outline.note: Zion is addressed as a woman in travail who will leave the city, come to Babylon, and there be rescued and redeemed.

outline.heading: Nations gathered for judgment
outline.note: Many nations gloat over Zion, but they do not know Yahweh’s counsel; Zion is commanded to thresh, and the nations’ gain is devoted to Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: Many nations will go and say, “Come! Let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For the law will go out of Zion, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem;
keyVerses.why: This verse names the chapter’s opening hope: nations come to Zion not first for tribute or conquest, but to be taught Yahweh’s ways.

keyVerses.text: and he will judge between many peoples, and will decide concerning strong nations afar off. They will beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will not lift up sword against nation, neither will they learn war any more.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter’s best-known peace vision, joining divine judgment with the end of learned warfare.

keyVerses.text: and I will make that which was lame a remnant, and that which was cast far off a strong nation: and Yahweh will reign over them on Mount Zion from then on, even forever.”
keyVerses.why: The verse shows that restoration centers on those described as lame and cast far off, not on the untouched strength of the powerful.

keyVerses.text: Be in pain, and labor to give birth, daughter of Zion, like a woman in travail; for now you will go out of the city, and will dwell in the field, and will come even to Babylon. There you will be rescued. There Yahweh will redeem you from the hand of your enemies.
keyVerses.why: This verse keeps the chapter’s hope honest: rescue is promised, but it comes through displacement and Babylon.

themes: The lame and driven away gathered
Yahweh’s counsel hidden from hostile nations

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with “the latter days”?
questions.answer: The phrase points the reader toward a future scene rather than Micah’s immediate present. In this chapter, that future includes Zion raised up, nations coming to learn, and warfare ending. The text does not give a calendar date for when these “latter days” occur.

questions.question: What is “the mountain of Yahweh’s temple”?
questions.answer: The phrase refers to Zion or Jerusalem as the place associated with Yahweh’s house in this vision. The mountain is pictured as established above other mountains, and peoples stream to it. The point in the chapter is not topography alone, but Zion becoming the source from which Yahweh’s teaching and word go out.

questions.question: Are the nations forced to come to Zion?
questions.answer: Verses 1-2 picture peoples and many nations streaming and speaking to one another: “Come! Let’s go up.” The chapter emphasizes their desire to be taught Yahweh’s ways. Later in the chapter, however, other nations assemble against Zion, so “the nations” are not presented in only one role.

questions.question: Does verse 3 simply mean there will be no more conflict anywhere?
questions.answer: Verse 3 envisions nations no longer lifting up sword against nation or learning war. Later the chapter describes nations assembled against Zion and Zion commanded to thresh them. These are distinct scenes of peace, siege, and judgment; the poem does not supply a complete chronology connecting them. The later conflict images remain part of the chapter alongside its opening hope for peace.

questions.question: What does it mean that each person sits under a vine and fig tree?
questions.answer: Verse 4 pictures settled security: every man sits under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one makes them afraid. The image is agricultural and domestic, not military. It follows the remaking of weapons into tools for cultivation.

questions.question: Why does verse 5 mention other gods after the nations have come to learn Yahweh’s ways?
questions.answer: Verse 5 contrasts the nations walking in the name of their gods with the speaker’s commitment to walk in the name of Yahweh. The line may sound like a present confession placed beside the future vision of verses 1-4, without fully explaining how that vision unfolds. Brenton’s English says the nations walk in their own way, where WEB refers to the names of their gods; the editions differ in this clause as well as in wording elsewhere.

questions.question: Who are “that which is lame” and “that which is driven away”?
questions.answer: The chapter describes them as people Yahweh will assemble and gather. Verse 7 says the lame become a remnant and the cast far off become a strong nation. The wording focuses on reversal: those marked by weakness, distance, or affliction are gathered under Yahweh’s reign on Mount Zion.

questions.question: Why is Babylon mentioned?
questions.answer: Verse 10 says the daughter of Zion will leave the city, dwell in the field, and come to Babylon. The same verse promises that there she will be rescued and redeemed from enemies. The book’s horizon thus includes Babylonian exile and restoration, beyond its heading’s eighth-century setting. Scholars differ over whether such passages reflect the named prophet’s foresight or later shaping of the collection. Within this scene, rescue is promised at the place of displacement.

questions.question: What is the image of threshing doing at the end?
questions.answer: Threshing is the process of separating grain from harvested stalks, and verse 12 says Yahweh has gathered the nations like sheaves to the threshing floor. Verse 13 then commands daughter of Zion to arise and thresh, using images of iron horn and bronze hoofs. The scene is violent judgment imagery, not a general permission for readers to attack enemies.

glossary.def: The future time introduced in verse 1, when Zion is exalted and nations stream to Yahweh’s mountain.
A name used in this chapter for Jerusalem as the place from which Yahweh’s law and word go out and as the city later threatened by nations.
The gathered survivors or restored group in verse 7, made from what was lame and cast far off.
The place named in verse 10 as the destination of Zion’s displacement and also the place where rescue and redemption are promised.
The action commanded in verse 13, using harvest-floor imagery for judgment on the gathered nations.
